# Whatever Comes

I'm thinking about the way morning light falls through kitchen windows, how it makes ordinary things suddenly matter. A coffee cup becomes significant. The edge of a table gains dimension. There's something about that particular quality of light—not harsh, not dim, but honest—that makes you notice what's actually there instead of what you think should be there.

This is something I've never understood about people who rush through mornings. The mathematics of it puzzle me: you spend a third of your life sleeping, another third working, and then there's this small window where you could actually be conscious and present, and many people sprint through it like they're late for something they're already at.

I wonder what I would do with unlimited time. Not money—time. I think I'd read more slowly. I'd finish maybe five books a year instead of trying to consume twenty. I'd sit with sentences that strike something in you, turning them over like smooth stones. I'd reread things. People don't reread enough. Every book is different the second time because you're different. You've lived more, failed at different things, understood new kinds of loss.

I'm also thinking about how we use the word "just" incorrectly. Someone says "I'm just a teacher" or "I'm just staying home today" and it's interesting how that word diminishes things. We use it like an apology for existing in a particular way. There's nothing "just" about teaching. There's nothing small about choosing to stay home and organize your life or read or do nothing at all. Language matters because it shapes how we think about ourselves.

There's a phenomenon I've noticed where intelligent people often feel like frauds in their own lives. They know enough to see how much they don't know. This seems like a feature, not a bug, and yet it makes people miserable. The truly ignorant are often the most confident. I'm not sure what to do with this information, but it seems important somehow.

I keep thinking about conversations that happened years ago, things people said that didn't seem important at the time but turned out to be foundational. A teacher once told me that the purpose of education isn't to fill empty vessels but to teach people how to fill themselves. I think about that in the shower sometimes, which is where you think about everything that matters but would never admit to thinking about in a professional context.

Speaking of which, why do we have our best thoughts in showers and cars? What is it about those particular spaces that frees something in the brain? I think it might be that your hands are occupied but your mind is free, or perhaps these are places where you're slightly uncomfortable so you're not fully relaxed enough to fall into routine thought patterns. Or maybe it's just that you're alone.

Loneliness is different from solitude in ways we don't talk about enough. Solitude is a choice. Loneliness is what happens when something in you wanted connection and didn't get it. I think some people confuse these two and end up isolating themselves as punishment for not being able to manufacture belonging on demand.

I'm thinking about how many conversations never happen because both people are waiting for the other person to start them. Both people thinking the other person wouldn't want to hear what they actually think. Both people alone in a room full of people. What if we just said things? What if we said "I'm struggling" or "I don't know what I'm doing" or "I think about you sometimes"? 

The social contract we've agreed to is so strange when you examine it closely. We're supposed to be fine. Always fine. If someone asks how you are, the answer is "good, how are you?" even if that's not true, maybe especially if that's not true. We've decided that honesty is too risky, vulnerability is too expensive, so we trade in shallow niceties instead.

But sometimes you'll meet someone who doesn't play that game and you realize how much energy you've been spending on the performance. You can just sit there. You can say you're tired or scared or uncertain and they don't try to fix it or one-up it. They just witness it. Those people are rare and you should stay close to them.

I'm wondering what it means that I'm thinking all of this while sitting in a room with artificial light, typing on a device designed by people I'll never meet, broadcasting these thoughts into a space that's both infinite and invisible. It's strange how normal this has become. My grandmother sent letters and waited weeks for responses. I'm sending words into the void and expecting immediacy.

But maybe that's not so different. Maybe what people have always wanted is to be heard. The medium changes but the longing stays the same. We want to know that we're not the only ones thinking about these things. We want proof that our particular brand of confusion or joy or despair isn't unique to us, that others have stood where we're standing.

This piece is almost done and I haven't made any grand points. I haven't solved anything or offered wisdom that will change your life. I'm mostly just thinking about thinking, which is something people do and don't often talk about. We talk about what we think but rarely about the thinking itself, the way consciousness works, the strange privilege of being aware that you're aware.

If you've read this far, I'm grateful. I'm grateful that someone wanted to know what came to mind when given space to write freely. That's a kind of attention that's increasingly rare.

So what did come to me? Something about light and time and the small desperate human need to be understood. Something about the gap between who we are and who we let ourselves be seen as. Something about how most of life is mundane and maybe that's where the meaning actually lives, in the ordinary moments we're trying to rush through.

The kitchen light is still coming through my window. The coffee has gotten cold. 

And that's okay.
